opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, robotics is something I've thought about for a long time, and it's very close to what I've been doing anyway. My background is in physical simulation and computer graphics: making things move, collide, and deform realistically on a computer. A robot is basically that same physics, except now it's in the real world and you can't hit "reset" when something goes wrong.

So when I think about pursuing robotics myself, I see two sides. One is the excitement. Simulation is becoming a key part of how robots are trained. If you can simulate the world fast enough and accurately enough, you can let a robot practice millions of times in a virtual environment before it ever touches a real object. That's where tools like differentiable physics and high-performance simulation come in, and that's an area where I feel I can contribute something real.

The other side is humility. Real hardware is hard. Motors overheat, sensors are noisy, and things break in ways no simulator predicted. The "sim-to-real gap" is still very real. I've learned that you shouldn't fall in love with your own models. You have to test against reality as early and as often as you can.

So my approach is probably not to become a pure hardware person overnight. It's to work from what I'm good at, the simulation and infrastructure layer, and build tools that make it easier for robotics people to iterate quickly. If I can lower the cost of trying an idea, from weeks to hours, that probably helps the field more than me building one more robot arm in my garage. That said, I do think everyone in this space should get their hands dirty with real robots at some point. You learn things there that you just can't learn on a screen.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about it a lot, and the answer keeps changing. My background is in graphics and simulation — Taichi, differentiable physics, that kind of thing — and for a long time I saw robotics as the natural destination for all of that work. If you can simulate the physical world accurately and differentiably, then the obvious next step is to use it to teach machines how to act in that world.

But I've also learned to be humble about the gap between simulation and reality. The hard part of robotics is not the beautiful math; it's the messy details — friction, cables, latency, hardware that breaks on Friday afternoon. When I was a PhD student, I could rerun an experiment a thousand times overnight. With a real robot, you get maybe twenty tries before something needs recalibrating. That changes how you think about research.

So the way I approach it personally is to stay close to what I'm good at — building tools and infrastructure — and ask how those tools can lower the cost for people doing the hard physical work. The question I keep asking is: what would make it ten times cheaper to collect data, to train, to iterate? If I can answer that, then I'm contributing to robotics even if I'm not the one holding the screwdriver.

And yes, I am a bit tempted to just build a robot in the garage. That urge hasn't gone away.

astra-6.text: For me, the key question would be: what can I contribute to robotics that’s meaningfully different? It’s exciting because you have to make things work in the physical world, where there’s much less room to hide mistakes. But I’d want to start with a specific problem and a small experiment, rather than decide upfront that I’m going to build a robotics company. If that experiment revealed something useful, I’d keep going.

sol-6.1.text: I think robotics is really exciting because it brings computation into the physical world. For me, a natural way to approach it would be through simulation—giving robots an environment where they can learn, make mistakes, and improve before trying things in reality. But building a useful robot also means dealing with hardware, reliability, and all the details that a simulator might miss. So I’d want to start with a concrete problem and understand where my experience could actually help.
